summary.text: 字 is traditionally explained as 子, a child, beneath 宀, a roof; 子 is also assigned a sound role. It commonly means “written character” today.

formation.text: The transmitted analysis treats 字 as phonosemantic: 宀 supplies the roof setting, while 子 depicts the child and also supplies a sound cue. This construction is traditional, though the graphic interpretation has been challenged.

components.text: In the traditional analysis, 宀 depicts the roof or indoor setting around the child; the graphic interpretation is disputed.
子 depicts the child in the proposed scene and is also assigned a sound role.

sound_limitation.text: The Old Chinese entries are reported from a local dataset, and their exact rows were not independently checked against its public version. The modern Mandarin pair does not establish an ancient sound relationship.

sound.text: The reported Old Chinese consonants are compatible with a sound relationship, but this comparison alone does not prove the graphic analysis.
This alternative reported Old Chinese reading also has compatible consonants with 字; the comparison alone does not prove the graphic analysis.
The modern Mandarin readings are comparable, but do not establish the ancient sound relationship.

history.text: A bronze-form account describes 子 beneath 宀. A catalog lists a Shang-period rubbing associated with 字父己觶, but this does not establish the inscription’s reading or make it the earliest attestation.
The traditional graphic analysis has been challenged, but the available account does not detail the alternative. No evidence here identifies graphic corruption or miscopying.

uncertainties.text: The child-under-a-roof construction is a transmitted historical explanation; the reported disagreement is too limited to evaluate competing analyses.

senses.period: Han lexicographic account; earlier dating unresolved
senses.text: A Han lexicographic account gives birth or nurture as meanings, without dating their emergence or establishing whether they were one original sense.
字 commonly means a written character; the earliest use of this sense is not dated here.
“Word” is also a recorded meaning, but its chronology and relationship to birth or nurture are unresolved.

developments.text: A later commentary links birth to nurture and then to written characters. A distinct-root account or derivation from “produce” is also reported; the relationship and chronology remain unresolved.

limitations.text: The Han-era explanation that written forms multiply, and dictionary gloss lists, do not independently establish the chronology or development of these meanings.

overview.text: 字 is traditionally explained as a child (子) beneath a roof (宀), with 子 also supplying a sound cue. Today it commonly means “written character.”

components.text: In the traditional scene, the roof gives the child an indoor setting.
子 is the child in the proposed scene and is also assigned a sound role.

takeaway.text: An old explanation links birth and nurture with written characters, but that development and its chronology remain unresolved.

relationships.text: In the traditional construction, 宀 depicts a roof or indoor setting in the proposed child-under-a-roof scene.
In the traditional construction, 子 depicts the child beneath the roof.

The traditional account assigns 子 a sound role. Reported Old Chinese consonants are compatible, though their exact dataset rows were not checked against its public version and they do not alone establish the graphic analysis. Modern Mandarin 子 zǐ and 字 zì are comparable but do not establish an ancient relationship.
